title: Where @SafeVarargs compiles, and what javac does with "all"

blocks.text: Questions on what this page has just taught. Choose one answer for each.

questions.stem: Which of these generic varargs methods may carry @SafeVarargs without a compile error in Java 21?

options.text: A public instance method of a class: public <T> void addAll(T... items).
options.says: A public instance method that is neither static nor final can be overridden, so @SafeVarargs on it is a compile error.

options.text: A private instance method of a class: private <T> void addAll(T... items).
options.says: Since Java 9 private instance methods qualify, because a private method cannot be overridden, like static and final methods and constructors.

options.text: A default method of an interface: default <T> void addAll(T... items).
options.says: A default method can be overridden and is not static, final or private, so @SafeVarargs on it is a compile error.

questions.stem: A method marked @SuppressWarnings("all") contains an unchecked cast and is compiled by javac with -Xlint:unchecked. What does javac do?

options.text: It reports the warning, because it ignores the key "all".
options.says: javac honours only its own -Xlint keys such as unchecked or deprecation and silently ignores any other string; "all" works only in IDEs and the Eclipse compiler.

options.text: It reports nothing, because "all" covers each warning category.
options.says: That is how IDEs and the Eclipse compiler read "all"; javac does not recognise the key, so nothing is suppressed.

options.text: It stops with an error, because "all" is an unknown key.
options.says: An unknown key is not an error for javac: the page says it silently ignores strings it does not know.

concepts: @SafeVarargs compiles only on static, final or private methods and on constructors, because other methods could be overridden unsafely.
@SuppressWarnings takes the narrowest key on the narrowest scope, and javac ignores keys it does not know, "all" included.
